newsitem.title: USA: U.S. congratulates East Timor Nobel prizewinners.
newsitem.headline: U.S. congratulates East Timor Nobel prizewinners.

text.p: The United States on Friday congratulated two East Timor independence campaigners who were awarded the 1996 Nobel Peace Prize and said it hoped the award would help efforts to settle problems in the territory.

"We congratulate these two men on winning this award," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said. "We hope that the action of conferring the award on them will lead to a resolution of the problems of East Timor in which the United States does have an interest."

The Norwegian Nobel Committee gave the award to Bishop Carlos Belo and resistance leader Jose Ramos-Horta, saying it was aimed at influencing the conflict that has festered since Indonesia invaded the former Portuguese territory in 1975.

Burns said the United States had expressed concern in the past over human rights conditions in Indonesian-ruled East Timor and would continue to do so. But he said Washington was going ahead with a deal to sell Indonesia nine F-16 fighters.
America has a "multifaceted" relationship with Jakarta and "will continue to have a very active and we hope positive relationship with the Indonesian government," he said.

"We have spoken out publicly about human rights abuses in East Timor and will continue to do so," Burns said, adding that Secretary of State Warren Christopher had made the U.S. case during a visit to Jakarta last summer.

The State Department's measured reaction reflected the middle course Washington has attempted to steer for years in its relations with Indonesia. It wants to maintain good ties with the world's most populous Moslem state, now a rising economic power in the region, but domestic pressures have forced criticisms of Jakarta's human rights policy.

Burns re-stated the obscurely worded U.S. official position on East Timor's legal status. "We accept Indonesia's incorporation of East Timor without maintaining that a valid act of self-determination has taken place," he said.

Indignation in Congress at an Indonesian government crackdown on opposition activists last July -- just after Christopher's visit there -- forced the administration to postpone the F-16 sale. But the State Department says it plans to go ahead with the sale in the New Year.
"We do balance our interests but we feel quite comfortable in going ahead with the sale of F-16s," Burns said.
